item.title: Avi Chawla NVIDIA released a new looped transformer: Instead of stacking more la
item.description:
Avi Chawla
NVIDIA released a new looped transformer:

Instead of stacking more layers, it runs the same layers multiple times so a 4B model can think like a 9B one.

Here's how it works:

In a standard transformer, every token passes through a stack of decoder blocks once, and each block has its own weights.

So if you want a deeper model, you add more blocks, and the parameter count grows with the depth.

NVIDIA's Dory1.0-4B decouples the two by reusing a chunk of its layers.

The model is split into three parts:

> An input block of 8 blocks runs once and turns the tokens into a hidden state x.

> A recurrent block of 20 shared blocks runs k times, where k can be anywhere from 1 to 4.

> An output block of 8 blocks runs once on the final state, followed by the LM head.

Before every pass through the recurrent block, x is added back to the current state and the sum is L2-normalized.

This keeps the original token representation in view on every pass, instead of each pass only seeing what the previous one produced.

Both models in the diagram below store 36 blocks of weights.

The standard transformer applies each block once, while Dory applies 36 blocks at k=1, 56 at k=2, and 96 at k=4, i.e., 72, 112, and 192 physical layers from the same checkpoint.

The extra depth is actually helpful on reasoning and agentic tasks:

> SWE-bench Verified:

- at 1 loop → 50.3
- at 2 loops → 59.5
- at 4 loops → 61.8

> 12-benchmark average:

- at 1 loop → 35.17
- at 2 loops → 39.67
- at 4 loops → 40.60
- and with 2 or more loops, it beats Qwen3.5-9B, Gemma 4 12B, and Gemma 4 26B-A4B.

More loops implies more compute per token, but the 4-loop model also writes 1.3x to 2.5x fewer output tokens on agentic tasks.

So 2 loops end up costing only 1.03x to 1.25x the compute of 1 loop end to end, which is why NVIDIA recommends 2 as the default.

By default, Dory keeps a separate KV cache for every loop, so at 4 loops the recurrent layers store 4x the cache.

To avoid this, it can keep only the cache from the last loop, which uses the same KV memory as a normal model with only a small change in accuracy.

One thing to note here is that looping helps the model reason over what it already knows, but it does not add knowledge.

For instance, on tasks like AA-Omniscience, accuracy stays at 10.0 whether you run 1 loop or 4, and on knowledge-heavy tasks like GPQA, Dory still trails Qwen3.5-4B.

Here's the paper: https://t.co/pdrqhdCHpZ

That said, how much memory looping costs comes down to how the KV cache is handled, so I wrote a full breakdown of how KV caching works.

It covers what gets cached during prefill, how the cache grows during decoding, and why it becomes the main memory bottleneck at long context.

Read it below.

https://t.co/HTVp6zvP3v - Avi Chawla

item.title: Daily Dose of Data Science 5 LLM fine-tuning techniques, explained with visuals:
item.description:
Daily Dose of Data Science
5 LLM fine-tuning techniques, explained with visuals:

Traditional fine‑tuning is impractical for LLMs (billions of params; 100s of GB).

Since this kind of compute isn't accessible to everyone, parameter-efficient fine-tuning techniques (PEFT) were built.

Before we go into details of each technique, here's some background that will help you better understand these techniques:

LLM weights are matrices of numbers adjusted during fine-tuning.

Most PEFT techniques involve finding a lower-rank adaptation of these matrices, a smaller-dimensional matrix that can still represent the information stored in the original.

Now with a basic understanding of the rank of a matrix, we're in a good position to understand the different fine-tuning techniques.

(refer to the image below for a visual explanation of each technique)

1) LoRA

- Add two low-rank trainable matrices, A and B, alongside the weight matrices.
- Instead of fine-tuning W, adjust the updates in these low-rank matrices.

Even for the largest LLMs, LoRA matrices take up a few MBs of memory.

2) LoRA-FA

While LoRA significantly decreases the total trainable parameters, it requires substantial activation memory to update the low-rank weights.

LoRA-FA (FA stands for Frozen-A) freezes matrix A and only updates matrix B.

3) VeRA

- In LoRA, low-rank matrices A and B are unique for each layer.
- In VeRA, A and B are frozen, random, and shared across all layers.
- Instead, it learns layer-specific scaling VECTORS (b and d) instead.

4) Delta-LoRA

- It tunes the matrix W as well, but not in the traditional way.
- Here, the difference (or delta) between the product of matrices A and B in two consecutive training steps is added to W.

5) LoRA+

- In LoRA, both matrices A and B are updated with the same learning rate.
- Authors of LoRA+ found that setting a higher learning rate for matrix B results in better convergence.

item.title: Rainier 这个update os还不行，因为mspaint不是通过windows update更新的，而是通过windows store更新的。 🤣 而且
item.description:
Rainier
这个update os还不行，因为mspaint不是通过windows update更新的，而是通过windows store更新的。🤣

而且这个安全漏洞非常离谱，mspaint，
画图？
这个不联网的画图，
居然有高达8.1分的rce远程执行漏洞？
黑客顺着网线爬过来吗？

那就要感谢，伟大的AI产品 copilot了。

因为天才的PM在最新版的paint中插入了copilot的功能。
她们想啊，如果小朋友想画一个草泥马🦙不会画，怎么办啊，我用copilot prompt一下，然后网上就能帮你找到图片就可以改改啦。
多么天才的想法。
这就给画图加上了copilot的功能，让mspaint 也变成一个联网的app。

而处理文件格式是各种系统最容易出安全漏洞的地方，苹果处理jpg格式就出过0click 0day。
那么很不巧，mspaint在设计的时候从未想过要联网，也从未做过这方面的security review，threat modeling。
然后正巧，mspaint中正好有一个文件解析的漏洞Out-of-bounds read。
然后连起来就是RCE.

利用难度很大，但是确实也是RCE。
用户用copilot让画图画一只草泥马，结果下载了一个恶意的图片，解析文件出错，执行了黑客的恶意代码。

Apps can't protect you from OS vulnerabilities. Update your OS immediately. - CZ 🔶 BNB
tweet

item.title: Akshay 🚀 RT @akshay_pachaar : I have been fine-tuning LLMs for over 3 years now!
item.description:
Akshay 🚀
RT @akshay_pachaar: I have been fine-tuning LLMs for over 3 years now!

Here’s how to train an LLM on tasks with multiple correct answers:

Consider a model that generates staff schedules.

Two schedules can look completely different while still being valid.

Both may cover every shift, respect employee availability, satisfy labor rules, and remain within budget.

There is no single completion that SFT should teach the model to imitate. What we do have is a set of rules that every valid schedule must satisfy.

This makes the problem a good fit for RLVR.

Amazon SageMaker AI supports this through its serverless model customization workflow and the new Training Sessions APIs.

Training Sessions keep the model loaded in a stateful GPU session while the engineer controls the RL loop, including rollout generation, reward computation, and policy updates.

SageMaker AI manages the underlying GPU infrastructure and distributed execution. The remaining challenge is converting the scheduling requirements into a verifier.

For example:

1. Is every shift covered?
2. Is anyone double-booked?
3. Are all labor rules satisfied?
4. Is the total cost within budget?

Inside this RL loop, the model generates several candidate schedules for each prompt.

The verifier runs the same four checks against every candidate.

For instance, a schedule passing all four checks can receive 1.0, passing three can return 0.75, and so on.

GRPO compares the rewards within each group and updates the model toward the higher-scoring schedules.

The model is therefore not learning one predefined schedule, but instead it is learning to produce schedules that satisfy the underlying specification.

The reward function still needs careful design.

An uncovered shift is not equivalent to exceeding the preferred cost by 1%.

A production verifier should treat coverage, double-booking, and labor rules as hard constraints. Any violation could return zero.

Cost and employee preferences can then act as soft constraints that rank the schedules that remain valid.

Consider a model that generates staff schedules.

There is no single completion that SFT should teach the model to imitate. What we do have is a set of rules that every valid schedule must satisfy.

This makes the problem a good fit for RLVR.

For example:

1. Is every shift covered?
2. Is anyone double-booked?
3. Are all labor rules satisfied?
4. Is the total cost within budget?

Inside this RL loop, the model generates several candidate schedules for each prompt.

The verifier runs the same four checks against every candidate.

For instance, a schedule passing all four checks can receive 1.0, passing three can return 0.75, and so on.

GRPO compares the rewards within each group and updates the model toward the higher-scoring schedules.

The model is therefore not learning one predefined schedule, but instead it is learning to produce schedules that satisfy the underlying specification.

item.title: 麦田 Rye 🇺🇦 RT @zstats : I have a particularly nasty case of cancer. When I was ho
item.description:
麦田 Rye 🇺🇦
RT @zstats: I have a particularly nasty case of cancer. When I was hospitalized again at my lowest point last year, I told Jensen. He immediately reached out to contacts at Stanford, who were able to cut through red tape, and get me into a clinical trial for which I've turned out to be a perfect fit. I think everyone can have their own views about recent events. But any claims that Jensen did not really care about his staff is simply inaccurate. I, personally, owe him more than I can express.

I think the best tribute we can pay to Jensen's legacy is to drive NVIDIA's continued success and push the whole industry forward, by showing we've learned the lessons from years of working here. We will compare ourselves against Speed of Light. The mission will be the boss. And we will not be scared to take smart, bold risks and fail fast with ruthless intellectual honesty.

But if there is one management story I remember the most, it's a particular Jensen grilling from my time in autonomous vehicles that stayed with me. Luckily I was not in the hot seat for this one. Team A didn't want to use Team B's framework, because they thought it was too slow. Jensen was surprised - it's just applying a bunch of optimized CUDA kernels in sequence, how could it be slow?

So he asked the executive from team B to draw the entire data flow sequence from their framework on the whiteboard and highlight every memcpy. Sure enough, there were a bunch of unnecessary memcpy's surrounding each pipeline stage. Everyone in the room could see why it wasn't getting to SoL and a path to improve things. No arguing about fiefdoms or appeals to authority - the data got us all on the same page.

The lesson was not (just) that unnecessary memory copying is bad. It's that executives should not be afraid to probe into details if something doesn't add up, and leaders need to be technical enough and honest enough to engage in real time and not turn every meeting into "I'll get back to you in a week." If that means counting memcpy's with a billionaire CEO, so be it.

My best executive meetings at NVIDIA have been when I'm fully prepared to present every detail of my team's work, and my worst failures have come when I realized I couldn't go deep enough to really solve the problem.

But the thing that gives me confidence is that Jensen was never the only one to live this philosophy. Anyone who has presented to an SVP at NVIDIA knows they are at risk for getting grilled on fundamental constraints and technical details. I have been part of amazing conversations with both recent and old timer leaders where we were able to get to the core of a problem in an hour rather than a month, because we had the right people in the room and were not afraid to go deeper.

The company is filled with supremely talented people who have been trained for 3 decades to work at the highest level, and you can see it in what we produce every day. I'm so proud to be an NVIDIAn, and I can't wait to show off what we ship in the coming months and years.
tweet
